Settings

Every knob on the device.

Players
3 to 15.
Imposters
How many of you're secretly lying. Half the players at most, so 8 players allows 4. One is plenty to start with.
Hint word
Word mode, in setup. The hint word is the single word an imposter gets instead of the real one. On: they get it. Off: they get only the category, which makes it a lot harder for them. The switch says which, so you're never guessing what it does.
Meetings
Tag mode, in setup. How many emergency meetings the whole group gets to share, up to nine, counted down on screen while you play. The meetings you call because you found somebody on the ground are free and never touch this number.
Light
Screen brightness, ten steps.
Theme
Nine looks to pick from, three on screen at a time with arrows to page through the rest. Paper and Frost are the light ones, and Mono is black on white, which is the one that holds up in bright sun.
Tips
The little helper line along the bottom of the screen, the one that says "Locked. Tap the padlock." when you tap a locked box. Leave it on for your first few games and turn it off once you know what everything does.
Lock
Arrives off. Off, Manual or Auto. Manual puts a padlock at the top of the screen that you shut yourself. Auto shuts it every time the box is handed on. While it's shut, nothing answers except the padlock. Turning the lock on or off asks you to confirm first. All of it here →
Home and settings
Top right of every screen once a game is under way, and on the menu the settings sliders sit in the middle of the top row instead. You're never more than one tap from either, and Back out of settings returns you to the screen you left.
Info
Top left of the menu. Nine pages: five short rule pages for whichever mode you tapped last, then your code for playing on a phone, the version your box is on, this page as a QR code, and the same address written out for when a phone won't read the code.
Battery
A percentage in settings, and a red badge on the menu once it is down to 20. Charge it with any USB-C cable. While it's plugged in that same tile says Charging, and the percentage comes back once you unplug it. The box dims after a minute of nobody touching it and blanks after ten, and a tap wakes it right where it was. It won't do either in the middle of a tag cooldown, because that screen is the game at that moment.
Screen
Says Normal or Flipped. Tap it to turn the picture upside down. The charging socket is on one end, so with a cable plugged in the box only reads the right way up from one side of the table. Flip it and it reads correctly from the other. Taps follow the picture, so everything stays where it looks like it is.
Power saver
A bar underneath the percentage on the battery screen. Tap it and the box gets less patient: it dims after thirty seconds instead of a minute, and blanks after five minutes instead of ten. Worth it on a long night out, unnecessary at a table. It stays how you left it.
Off
Top right of the menu. Tapping it turns the backlight off and blanks the screen, and a tap on the glass brings it back exactly where you left it. There's no power switch on this one, so that's what off means here. It's still sipping a little in the background, so plug it in between game nights the way you would anything else with a battery in it.
Reveal
End of a round. In word mode it shows the word and which players were lying. In tag mode there's no word, so it just names the imposters.
The six tiles behind the sliders

Light, Theme, Battery, Tips, Lock and Screen. That's the whole settings page, and it is one page, not a list you scroll. Players, imposters, the hint switch and meetings aren't in here, because you set those on the way into a game instead.

The word bank

Eighteen categories and 450 words, the everyday sort a room full of people all know without explaining: animals, food, places, sports, jobs, school and plenty more. Every word carries five possible hints and each hint is a single word, so nothing gets cut off on a screen this small. The box won't deal a word it has already dealt in the last 16 rounds.
